purpose: Deferoxamine is used to remove excess iron from your body, which can build up to dangerous levels in people who receive frequent blood transfusions or accidentally swallow too much iron. It is also sometimes used to remove excess aluminum in people with kidney disease. Getting rid of this excess metal helps protect your heart, liver, and other organs from damage.
how_it_works: Think of deferoxamine like a tiny magnet that travels through your body and grabs onto iron or aluminum molecules that do not belong there. Once it latches onto these metals, it forms a harmless complex that your kidneys and bowels can then flush out of your body through your urine and stool. This process is called chelation, and it slowly and safely lowers the dangerous metal levels in your blood and tissues.
common_side_effects: Pain, swelling, or redness at the injection site are very common. You may notice your urine turning an orange-red or reddish-brown color — this is normal and harmless. Other common effects include flushing, stomach upset, nausea, diarrhea, leg cramps, and headache. Some people experience dizziness or a fast heartbeat, especially if the medicine is given too quickly.
warnings: Tell your doctor right away if you have trouble hearing or notice any vision changes, as this medicine can sometimes affect your eyesight and hearing with long-term use. It should be used very carefully in people with kidney problems. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor before using this medication. Children on long-term therapy may experience slowed bone growth. Never stop or change your dose without talking to your healthcare provider first.
typical_dosing: Deferoxamine is given as an injection, either under the skin (subcutaneous), into a muscle, or into a vein — it is not taken by mouth. For chronic iron overload, it is often given slowly under the skin over 8 to 12 hours using a small pump, typically 5 to 7 nights per week. For acute iron poisoning, it is given by a healthcare provider directly into the vein in a hospital setting. Your exact dose will be determined by your doctor based on your weight and iron levels.
